transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Leah Thompson (Cascade AI - Head of ML), Priya Singh (Lead ML Eng), Marco Ruiz (Infra)

Summary: quick technical review of quantization tradeoffs (GPTQ vs AWQ vs INT8/FP8), runtime implications (latency/throughput), KV cache and batching behavior, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Customer wants to understand accuracy regressions and recommended path for a POC.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right, hi everyone, thanks for joining. Maya from Redwood here, i'm the account owner, with ravi our se. uh thanks for making time.
[00:06] Leah Thompson: thanks, maya. we were excited to dig into quantization options, especially given our latency budget for inference.
[00:12] Ravi Patel: cool, i'll kick off with the high level then we can dive into the numbers. quick question, are you primarily running 4k context customer prompts or do you have some longer doc synthesis workloads?
[00:21] Priya Singh: mostly 2k to 4k, a few jobs at 8k for summarization. typical request size is ~400 tokens for our customer-facing assistant.
[00:28] Marco Ruiz: infrastructure note — for POC we'd prefer dedicated instances, ideally in our VPC. we have strict key management requirements, so KMS/HSM is mandatory.
[00:36] Ravi Patel: got it. so quantization: we'll compare GPTQ, AWQ, and our INT8 profiles; also touch on FP8 as an option for training/FP8 inference where available. quick TL;DR: AWQ often yields better perf on Ampere/Turing GPUs with lower accuracy drop on many tasks, but results vary by model and workload. GPTQ tends to be more conservative on accuracy but sometimes slower at runtime due to dequant/decode overhead if not using optimized kernels.
[01:00] Leah Thompson: can you quantify "better perf"? like latency and throughput improvements?
[01:03] Ravi Patel: sure. from our internal benches on Llama-2-style models: AWQ can reduce memory footprint ~2-2.5x vs FP16 and produce 20-35% latency reduction and up to 1.6-2x throughput in streaming scenarios when combined with continuous batching and KV prefix cache. GPTQ typically gives 1.5-1.8x memory reduction, latency gains 10-20%, but some workloads see a 0.5-1.5% absolute drop in certain NLU accuracy metrics depending on the task. those are broad numbers — per-model numbers matter.
[01:39] Priya Singh: what about INT8 (dynamic/static) vs AWQ?
[01:42] Ravi Patel: our INT8 path (quantization-aware static) is very stable for transformer weights when using calibrated ranges; it gives predictable latency but sometimes larger accuracy regressions than AWQ on decoder-only models. INT8 + tuned KV cache and attention kernel selection works well for throughput-heavy batch workloads. AWQ is more weight-centric and often keeps activations in higher precision which helps quality.
[02:04] Marco Ruiz: you mentioned FP8 — do you support FP8 kernels in our Dedicated stack? we run A100s.
[02:09] Maya Chen: FP8 is still spotty; some vendors have beta FP8 kernels on A100s and H100s. Redwood can enable FP8 where the kernel is stable but we'd treat it as experimental in POC — i.e., we'd run FP8 in parallel to other quant strategies but not recommend it for production until we see consistent evals.
[02:26] Leah Thompson: ok. accuracy regressions — we can't drop more than 1% on our intent classification F1, otherwise downstream user-experience suffers. what have you seen?
[02:34] Ravi Patel: in our experience, AWQ on Llama-like models tends to be within 0.2-0.8% F1 delta on intent tasks, GPTQ can be 0.0-1.5% depending on tuning and per-layer groupings. INT8 sometimes hits 1-3% on edge cases. caveat: these numbers depend heavily on prompt distribution and golden set. also some failure modes are brittle — hallucination increase or tokenization boundary errors.
[02:57] Priya Singh: how do you measure accuracy regressions? do you rerun on our golden set?
[03:01] Ravi Patel: yes, recommended workflow: you provide 2-3 prompt sets + golden outputs. we run AWQ, GPTQ, and INT8 on your exact workload, measure EM/F1/rouge (whatever you prefer) and also compute regression deltas. we'll include distribution charts so you can see per-prompt deltas, not just averages.
[03:17] Marco Ruiz: runtime implications — if we enable AWQ on Dedicated nodes, will KV cache behavior change? we rely on prefix KV cache heavily to hit latency SLOs.
[03:24] Ravi Patel: good question. KV cache is largely orthogonal to weight quantization — the cache stores activations / key-value tensors at runtime. but there are interactions: if quantization changes activation scaling or the attention kernel paths, the runtime may choose different optimized kernels which affects cache hit latency and memory accounting. practically what we observe is: with AWQ + optimized kernels, cold-start latency can be slightly higher due to dequant steps the first time a layer runs, but warm prefix cache access is usually unchanged and often faster overall because lower memory pressure allows larger batching without spilling. there are also cases where naive quantized kernels do extra memcpy which hurts micro latency; we tune around that.
[04:07] Leah Thompson: and batching? our traffic is bursty — sometimes many small requests in parallel. Will quantization allow better batching?
[04:14] Ravi Patel: lower memory footprints let the runtime pack more contexts into a single batch which improves throughput and avg latency under load. continuous batching + adaptive timeout heuristics are important for bursty workloads. AWQ usually enables slightly larger batch windows before hitting memory limits. but we need to tune the batching timeouts carefully so you don't increase tail latency for single-user flows.
[04:34] Maya Chen: can i interject on deployment options? For your VPC-onprem ask, Redwood Private supports customer-managed network and KMS. we can run the control plane in our cloud but connect to your VPC, or we can do full on-prem with our bundle. Marco, you mentioned HSM — we integrate with common HSMs (AWS CloudHSM, Thales) but we'll need an architecture diagram to confirm firewall rules.
[04:54] Marco Ruiz: yep i'll send our security doc after this. are there any known compatibility gaps with H100 vs A100 for AWQ/GPTQ?
[05:01] Ravi Patel: H100 tends to have better tensor core support for FP8 and some int8 kernels, which can increase throughput by another 10-25% for certain kernels. AWQ's optimized kernels can exploit those tensor cores more effectively. but some AWQ toolchains are still newer on H100, so we test both. A100 is stable for AWQ and INT8 in our Dedicated infra.
[05:20] Priya Singh: what about streaming / token latency? our assistant streams partial answers — we need token-level latencies below 120ms 95th.
[05:28] Ravi Patel: streaming introduces constraints: decoding loop and KV cache access per token. quantization reduces computation per token which helps hitting that 95th percentile, but microsecond-level overheads (memcpy, dequant) can add up. in practice we saw AWQ combined with optimized attention kernels and prefix caching hit ~90-100ms 95th for 2k contexts on A100 for models ~13B with continuous batching tuned. your mileage will vary on model and prompt length. we'll include token-level p95 in the bench output.
[06:01] Leah Thompson: are there any non-obvious failure modes?
[06:04] Ravi Patel: yes — common ones: (1) quantization-induced tokenization drift where a model prefers slightly different tokens leading to downstream metric drift, (2) quantized kernels sometimes expose numerical edge cases for very long sequences, (3) per-layer group sizes in GPTQ matter — naive grouping can amplify regression. We usually run per-layer reconstructions and an eval harness to catch these.
[06:25] Priya Singh: do you support mixed precision flows? like keep first/last layers fp16 and quantize middle?
[06:30] Ravi Patel: absolutely — middle-out quantization (selective per-layer) is common. AWQ and GPTQ toolchains both support selective codec where embedding and LM head are kept in higher precision to preserve quality. that's often the sweet spot: 90-95% of memory gains with minimal accuracy hit.
[06:45] Marco Ruiz: network overhead for Private — if we do VPC peering, is there any egress for model weights?
[06:50] Maya Chen: for Private full on-prem there is no egress; for VPC-connected Dedicated we stream model weights into the instance inside your VPC — initial weight transfer happens once and can be pinned. future updates can be controlled via your approval.
[07:01] Leah Thompson: ok great. can we see a sample benchmark output from a past POC?
[07:06] Maya Chen: yes, ravi will share an anonymized AWQ vs GPTQ spreadsheet with latency, throughput, memory, and per-prompt accuracy deltas.
[07:12] Ravi Patel: i'll attach that to the follow-up. quick note on instrumentation — we log token-level latencies and per-request model variant, so you can correlate regressions to requests. logs include trace IDs for debugging. 
[07:24] Priya Singh: what about toolchain time? generating GPTQ checkpoints can be long; how long does it take for say a 13B model?
[07:31] Ravi Patel: local GPTQ runs on a single A100 for 13B typically take 30-90 minutes depending on group size and reconstruction steps; AWQ toolchain is usually faster because it uses different heuristics and can run in 10-30 minutes. for POCs we often provide prebuilt AWQ artifacts for the common model families to save time.
[07:53] Marco Ruiz: any licensing or legal gotchas with quantization artifacts? we need to ensure model license compliance if we produce new quantized binaries.
[07:59] Maya Chen: good point. Redwood's policy is to treat quantized outputs as derivates — we track provenance and include model and toolchain metadata. we'll surface licensing notes in the follow-up.
[08:10] Leah Thompson: ok can you walk through the proposed POC plan?
[08:13] Maya Chen: proposed POC: 2-week micro-POC. Phase 1 (days 1-3): instrument and collect representative prompts + golden outputs from you. Phase 2 (days 4-9): run AWQ, GPTQ, INT8 on Dedicated trial nodes inside your VPC, collect latency/throughput/token-p95, and accuracy metrics. Phase 3 (days 10-14): provide report + a recommendation for production config and a canary rollout plan. we'll include rollback/fallback to higher-precision variants.
[08:41] Priya Singh: sounds good. what's the cost for Dedicated trial?
[08:44] Maya Chen: we'll include pricing in the follow-up; for POC we can provide limited trial credits but if you want longer runs we'll propose a short reserved capacity commitment.
[08:54] Marco Ruiz: one more question: how do you handle canary rollouts with quantized models? can we keep fp16 as fallback and automatically reroute if quality drops?
[09:02] Ravi Patel: yes — Redwood supports model variants and smart routing. you can do a canary where 5-10% traffic hits AWQ, compare metrics in real time, and if quality drops past thresholds we auto-failover to fp16 model. routing can be by route, user cohort, or latency.
[09:17] Leah Thompson: perfect. any security specifics we should be aware of?
[09:20] Maya Chen: we'll share SOC2 docs, the HSM integration notes, and our audit log schema.
[09:26] Priya Singh: timeline — we want to kick POC early October if possible.
[09:29] Maya Chen: we'll follow up with dates; aiming week of Oct 11 for scoping call and start shortly thereafter.
[09:36] Maya Chen: OK quick recap of action items and i'll hand it to ravi to close.
[09:40] Ravi Patel: thanks all. i'll run the initial microbenchmarks as soon as you send the prompts. expect a 2-3 day turnaround for the first pass.
[09:47] Leah Thompson: thanks everyone.
[09:49] Maya Chen: thanks, bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words ("k-v cash" for KV cache, "g p t q" spaced out), filler words kept. References: will attach AWQ_vs_GPTQ_microbench.xlsx, Redwood_Private_deploy_overview.pdf, POC_template.docx in follow-up email.
